extracted.intended_audience: patentees, inventors, patent agents, and patent lawyers (United Kingdom, late 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for obtaining, drafting, prosecuting, enforcing, amending, and revoking patents under the UK regime (Act of 1883 and supplements). Covers patentable subject-matter, specification and claims drafting, procedure before the Patent Office and courts, oppositions, assignments, infringement and remedies, and international/colonial issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter / nature of patentable invention
rubrics_metrics.description: What kinds of things may be patented: e.g., 'manner of new manufactures'; excludes a 'bare principle'. Includes processes, new contrivances applied to new objects or purposes, new contrivances for well-known objects, new combinations of known parts or old processes, a new mode of applying a known thing, and chemical processes (sometimes combined with mechanical contrivances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bare principles are not patentable. Novel application of general principles to manufacture may be patentable. The rule as to applications does not necessarily apply to chemical cases. New shapes, modes of application, or combinations may be patentable so long as the novelty is in the application or result and not merely an obvious rearrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (incident of utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility is a necessary incident of a patentable invention: the invention must be useful in some practicable sense; 'does not mean abstract utility'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent for a useless invention is void. The slightest amount of utility is sufficient. Utility must be judged by the state of things at the date of the patent. Lack of commercial success is not necessarily proof of want of utility, though failure to work the invention may be primâ facie evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / prior publication and public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior publication, prior public use, or prior public drawings/description that make the invention part of public knowledge will avoid patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published drawings or prior specifications may invalidate later patents. Prior imperfect machines or experimental use do not necessarily defeat novelty; scope of permissible experiments is limited. Confidential communications or secret use by the inventor under some circumstances do not constitute public disclosure. Publication abroad has specific rules; the International Convention affects priority/publication consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: True and first inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent should be vested in the true and first inventor (or those rightly entitled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations of who is the true and first inventor affect entitlement; proceedings address rival applicants and trustees where appropriate. Being the first inventor is a substantive ground in petitions / disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be a patentee (entitlement and joining non-inventors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-inventors may join with inventors in applying for a patent; rules govern who may be patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act permits non-inventors to be joint applicants; questions of entitlement and assignment must be resolved if rival claims arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title of the patent/specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Every specification (provisional and complete) must begin with a title; the invention and specification must fall within the title and the Comptroller may require amendment of the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title and specification are read together. The title should accurately indicate the subject-matter and any amendment may be required by the Examiner/Comptroller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional specification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional specification must describe the nature of the invention, begin with a title, include drawings if required, and ought not to comprise more than one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional specs are reported on by examiners and may be amended; acceptance is notified; after acceptance, invention may be used/published without prejudice to the patent. The provisional and complete specifications have limited relations: the complete must not materially add to or deviate from the provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete specification requirements (form and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The complete specification must commence with the title, end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed, and must be left with the application (or within the permitted period, typically nine months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete specifications are referred to examiners, may be required to be amended by the Comptroller, and if not left within due time the application may be deemed abandoned. The complete must be substantially the same as the provisional; developments within scope allowed but not material additions beyond the provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith and full disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Good faith must be observed in the specification; full disclosure of the invention is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee should fully disclose what he claims to have invented. Where invention was partly communicated from abroad, that should be distinguished. Failure to disclose (or misrepresentation) can be ground for revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and accuracy of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of the invention in the specification must be accurate so the reader may understand what it consists of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An accurate, precise definition is required so that the limits and scope are ascertainable; when patent is for improvements on an earlier patent, they must be clearly distinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency / enablement (means of carrying into effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must fully describe the means of carrying the invention into effect, not be vague or general, and must precisely describe materials and ingredients where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must describe the best method known of operating (best method rule) and must communicate the latest information. It need not set forth every application but must be intelligible to workmen of ordinary skill in the art. Failure of sufficiency is a ground for invalidity/revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims — presence, clarity, and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must end with a distinct statement of the invention claimed (claims). Claims should show clearly what is intended to be claimed; everything not claimed is impliedly disclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are not intended to aid the description. If all parts are old, only the combination should be claimed; new parts and minor combinations must be expressly claimed. Claims must not cover too much; vague or speculative claims are to be avoided; a large number of claims is dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity, misdirection and multiple methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity should be eschewed; the specification must not set forth two methods when only one is effective and must not contain misdirections or misrepresentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid statements that leave the skilled reader uncertain; misdirections are substantive problems and may render the specification deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must be provided where required to describe and ascertain the nature of the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings form part of the specification. Published drawings may affect novelty (a published drawing may avoid patentability). Drawings should be clear and sufficiently explanatory of structural features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation / construction of specification and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules govern the construction of the specification and the interpretation of the claims — how courts and examiners construe the language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction looks to description, title, and claims together; principles for claim construction and limits on interpretation are drawn from case law and statutory framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to specifications may be allowed (Comptroller/Board/Law Officers review and decide) but amendments must not enlarge or materially alter the original invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications for leave to amend are decided in first instance by the Comptroller and on appeal by a Law Officer; conditions and limitations differ under various Acts and rules. The Master or Court may grant leave in judicial proceedings, subject to limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties may oppose the grant of patents; the rules set who is entitled to oppose and the forms and grounds of opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions are decided by the Comptroller subject to appeal to a Law Officer; the manual details who may oppose, the modes of opposition, and consequences (such as refusal or amendment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sealing and dating of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are to be sealed by the Comptroller with the seal of the Patent Office within prescribed time limits (generally within fifteen months of application) and dated as of the day of application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sealing may be delayed by appeal, opposition, or the death of applicant. Special extensions of time may be allowed in particular circumstances; the sealed patent is the official grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and extension (prolongation) of letters patent
rubrics_metrics.description: There are procedures to extend or prolong the term of a patent (petition, hearings, accounts, costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions are subject to petition and judicial procedural hearings; costs and accounting consequences (e.g., payments or accounts) are prescribed and described in the manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments, licences, and registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments and licences of patents must follow procedural formalities and registration; registration particulars are prescribed and registration is necessary to enable assignee to maintain infringement actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments should be entered in the register to give notice to the world; registration relates back to date of assignment. Exclusive licence for a district is not notice to the world unless registered. Forms and fees apply. Fraudulent entries are penalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory licences
rubrics_metrics.description: The law recognizes compulsory licences subject to statutory grounds and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise sets out the grounds and procedure under which compulsory licensing may be ordered and the effects of such orders (e.g., terms, payments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement doctrines and scope of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for what constitutes infringement: e.g., where the principle is not new, invention of improvements is not a defence, combinations, chemical processes and products, dealing in articles made by infringing a patent, user infringement, liability of agents/carriers/foreign vessels/the Crown, and cases of non-infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intention of the infringer is not material. The manual explains tests for infringement, including construction of claims, equivalents, indirect infringement (dealing in), and special rules for chemical inventions and processes; many case examples illustrate these principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and procedure in actions for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules for litigating infringement: concurrent actions against several infringers, issues, inspection of machines and processes, particulars of breaches, trial practice, use of models, evidence, and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may order inspection, appoint referees for factual issues, determine issues of fact and law, and award costs. Specific procedural forms and case law examples guide practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies — injunctions, damages, account of profits, delivery up
rubrics_metrics.description: Available remedies for infringement include injunctions, damages, account of profits, delivery up or destruction of infringing articles, and other equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual discusses measure of damages, account of profits procedures, interlocutory relief (interim injunctions), and factors affecting quantum and discretion of the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation (repeal) of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds and procedure for revocation of patents: scire facias abolished; revocation by petition with prescribed grounds and respondents; trial procedure similar to infringement actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions for revocation can be presented by specified persons; service rules apply; courts may call on assessors; Court may allow patentee to apply to amend specification in revocation proceedings; costs follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offences and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal or statutory offences and penalties related to patents and the Patent Office (e.g., falsification of registers, unauthorized assumption of Royal Arms, misdemeanors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsification of the patent register is a misdemeanor; unauthorized use of protected insignia or false representation carries penalties specified in statutes and rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Convention and colonial arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: International and colonial patent arrangements (International Convention and Protocol) and summaries of foreign and colonial patent laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The International Convention affects priority and publication issues; prior use/publication abroad has rules and may or may not affect UK patentability. The Appendix contains summaries of foreign laws and colonial variations which practitioners must consult for overseas protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office rules and administrative practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Board of Trade (Patent Office) rules, examiners' reports, forms, registers, publications, and the public library constitute administrative practice; Board rules have the same effect as part of the Act unless annulled by Parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners report on form and substance; Comptroller may reject or require amendment; applicants have appeal rights to Law Officers; fees and forms are prescribed; registers and publications are public and evidentiary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent agents and Institute of Patent Agents (registration and conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation and registration of patent agents; rules governing entry in register of patent agents; Institute of Patent Agents matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Register of Patent Agents exists under rules; the Institute of Patent Agents administers certain functions; unregistered persons may be restricted from certain practice; rules and forms for registration and disciplinary matters are set out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees, forms, and procedural timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Schedules of government fees, forms to be used, and prescribed sizes/timings for documents (e.g., filing times, sealing times, fee reductions, and annual fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees were reduced and spread into annual sums under the Acts; specific fees and forms are enumerated. Timelines include periods for leaving complete specifications, sealing, extensions on death or appeal, and time-limits for oppositions and amendments.
